objectives: Measure which keys move when a node is added.
Distinguish key distribution from request-skew and real data migration.
retrieval: L059: why does a cache change work rather than ownership?
L061–068: distinguish partition assignment, replica placement and moving authoritative state.

sections.title: A bounded implementation milestone
sections.markdown: Scheduled60 minutes: brief/prediction10, implementation25, tests15, evidence10. Setup is separate. Partitioning is not complete when a hash returns a node name. This milestone isolates the placement question so you can test it before discussing migration. The supplied function uses highest-score rendezvous hashing: compute a stable score for each key/node pair and choose the greatest. Adding a new node changes a key's owner only if the new node wins that key's comparison. Existing scores do not change.

sections.title: Mechanism and correctness boundary
sections.markdown:
Use hashlib.sha256 rather than Python's built-in hash, whose process-dependent behavior is unsuitable for stable cross-process placement. Evaluate 1,000 distinct keys on nodes a,b, then on a,b,c. Count moved keys and assert every moved key now belongs to c. The test also checks a broad movement interval to catch obvious implementation mistakes, but the structural invariant is more important than memorizing an exact percentage.

This simulation does not copy database rows, prevent an old owner from accepting writes, or route reads during movement. A real migration needs a versioned ownership map, copy/catch-up behavior, an authoritative switch boundary, and stale-owner protection. A source that still accepts writes after a naive copy can diverge from the target. Explain the missing mechanisms before presenting the placement demonstration as architecture evidence.

Uniform distinct keys also do not imply uniform requests. A viral code may receive most accesses and still map to one node. Caching, replication of reads, or a product-specific split can help, but adding a node does not split that single key in this model. P1.4 later measures this skew explicitly.

sections.title: Use the prepared learner skeleton
sections.markdown:
Read projects/P1.md and projects/README.md. Edit projects/learner/shortener.py; the TODOs identify this milestone. Run the focused acceptance test from the repository root:

~~~powershell
$env:ACADEMY_LAB_IMPLEMENTATION = 'learner'
py -3 -m unittest discover -s projects/tests -p test_projects.py -k P1_3 -v
Remove-Item Env:ACADEMY_LAB_IMPLEMENTATION
~~~

The default test implementation is the completed reference; setting the variable selects your learner code. A learner TODO failure is intentional, not missing teaching. If your launcher is python or python3, substitute it for py -3. The baseline uses only the Python standard library and temporary test databases. No app endpoint executes your code.

Hash distribution balances distinct keys, not accesses. Repeating a viral key still concentrates requests on one owner; adding nodes alone does not split that key.

Stop when the focused test passes and you have recorded the stated evidence. Do not spend the hour constructing a new server framework or extending unrelated features.

sections.title: Record what the test actually shows
sections.markdown:
Show every moved key selects the new node; report moved fraction and distinguish the simulation from a storage migration.

Save the exact command, expected result, actual result, fault injected and the final invariant in the Project workspace. Note any untested assumption. The reference implementation and test have been executed; your own implementation needs its own run evidence. Compare with the explicit reference only after attempting the bounded task.

Single-machine SQLite, immutable links, an in-process cache, and a teaching HTTP harness. No abuse classifier, cross-node replication, account service, or distributed migration is implemented.

Optional additional practice belongs in a separate session: Add authenticated mutable destinations using versions and cache invalidation tests.

exercise.prompt: Implement highest-score rendezvous assignment using SHA-256 of key plus node. Compare 1,000 keys on two nodes versus three. Identify which assignments change and explain why actual migration needs ownership epochs and read/write handoff.
rubric: A code names exactly one immutable destination; successful create survives restart. Cache loss may add latency but cannot change a redirect.
Show every moved key selects the new node; report moved fraction and distinguish the simulation from a storage migration.
Reports the implemented guarantee and its limits.
exercise.solution: Compute one stable SHA-256 digest for each key/node pair, choose the node with the maximum digest, and reject an empty node list. Preserve the same serialization of the key and node across all participants. For each of the 1,000 keys compare its old and new owner; a changed assignment must choose the newly added node c because the old a/b scores are unchanged. Record moved count and per-node assignment counts. Then state the boundary: this is a placement simulation, so no data was copied and no writes were fenced. A real migration must preserve authoritative state through copying and the ownership switch, and a hot key remains concentrated even when average key counts look balanced.
